title: Day after crossover, legislative caucuses join together to advocate for bills — and each other
summary: Members of six legislative caucuses made history last year when they came together under the theme “We are Maryland.” Tuesday, they were joined by a seventh, the Legislative Muslim Caucus, to outline their goals “down the stretch” and to amplify unity.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters March 25, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters March 25, 2026

With less than three weeks left in the 2026 session, Maryland lawmakers who are members of legislative caucuses held a joint press conference Tuesday to outline their priorities “down the stretch” and to amplify unity.

The six caucuses made history last year when they came together for the first time under the theme “We are Maryland.” Tuesday, they were joined by a seventh caucus – the Legislative Muslim Caucus – that launched Feb. 16, on Muslim Lobby Day in Annapolis.

“I think that now we have a seat at the table, our voice is definitely going to be more valuable than anything else,” said Del. Sean Stinnett (D-Baltimore City), chair of the Muslim Caucus. The other two Muslim Caucus members are Dels. Sarah Wolek (D-Montgomery) and Caylin Young (D-Baltimore City).

“As you see here, we’re all inclusive in terms of working together and be able to build and making sure that the voices of all of us, not only Muslim, Jewish and so forth, are elevated,” Stinnett said.

The Muslim Caucus now joins the other six caucuses: the Asian American and Pacific Islanders (AAPI), Black, Jewish, Latino, LGBTQ+ and Women’s. They came together this year one day after the legislature’s crossover day, the date by which a bill has to pass out of one chamber to be guaranteed a hearing in the other.

Despite the tight calendar, there is still time for the caucuses to achieve their goals, said Del. Jared Solomon (D-Montgomery), co-chair of the Jewish Caucus.

“We’re not done. We’ve all seen bills literally pass at 11:55 [p.m.] on sine die, so there’s plenty of time left,” Solomon said Tuesday.

They have already notched at least one win: All the caucuses supported a ban on the so-called 287(g) programs. That bill was signed into last month, prohibiting cooperative agreements between Immigrations and Customs Enforcement and local law enforcement.

Although some local sheriffs support such agreements as a way to keep communities safe, the majority Democratic legislature and advocates said ICE under the Trump administration has aggressively targeted and arrested people from immigrant communities, some with limited or no criminal history.

“That is monumental,” said Del. Teresa Woorman (D-Montgomery), who spoke on behalf the Latino Caucus. Woorman, who came to the U.S. as a child from Mexico, and become a bit emotional when speaking about the change.

One piece of legislation supported by the caucuses is the Community Trust Act (Senate Bill 791/House Bill 1575). The bills sponsored by Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard) and Del. N. Scott Phillips (D-Baltimore County) would prohibit law enforcement agencies and jails from detaining individuals based on immigration status unless there was a judicial warrant to do so. Local officials would not be allowed to act based on administrative warrants from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the Justice Department “or any successor agency.”

So far, however, neither bill has moved out of committee.

“We spent a lot of time on a number of immigration-related bills very, very early in the session, and so that takes a lot of energy,” said Phillips, chair of the Black Caucus. “I think when many of us look around at what’s happening with those persons in our communities, in our districts, it’s still worth the fight.”

In the Trump administration’s second year, some caucus members called the federal government’s policies “cruel” and “reckless.”

Del. Dana Jones (D-Anne Arundel), chair of the Women’s Caucus, summarized how the administration in one year cut funding for Medicaid, clinics and the possible closure of labor and delivery units in rural communities.

“The list goes on and on as to the attack the federal government is taking on women throughout this country, but also here on Maryland’s women,” she said.

Some caucuses backed legislation (House Bill 560 and Senate Bill 308) that would require the governor to proclaim January as Muslim American Heritage Month and May as Jewish American Heritage Month.

The House version sponsored by Wolek and Solomon was approved by the full House Monday on a 126-7 vote. It now goes to the Senate’s Education, Energy and the Environment Committee, which has yet to act on SB 308, sponsored by Sen. Shelly Hettleman (D-Baltimore County), co-chair of the Jewish Caucus.
